Müller et al. (2020); Venus + Earth gravity assists shape the orbit toward 33° heliographic inclination over the mission lifetime, no chemical OI burn. Perihelion ~76 M km from Sun (above schema km cap; recorded in i18n description).

Cape Canaveral SLC-41, 2020-02-10. ESA-led mission with NASA launch + two instruments (SoloHI and the Heavy Ion Sensor). Solar Orbiter is the first spacecraft designed to image the Sun's polar regions in detail — a view inaccessible from Earth or any prior ecliptic-bound observatory.
Centaur upper stage burn places Solar Orbiter onto a Venus-encounter trajectory for the inclination-shaping phase.
2020-06-15. First close approach: 0.51 AU (~109 R☉). Initial science observations during Mercury's neighbourhood.
2022-09-04. Third VGA tilts the orbital plane upward, beginning the climb out of the ecliptic toward the polar viewing geometry.
2022-10-12. Reached 0.29 AU (~62 R☉) — within Mercury's perihelion distance. First close-approach observations using the full instrument suite.
2025-02. Fourth VGA continues raising heliographic latitude toward ~17° (extended mission target ~33°).

2025 onwards. Heliographic latitude exceeds 17° — the first close-up imaging of the Sun's polar magnetic field structures. The polar geometry is the unique scientific deliverable, complementary to Parker Solar Probe's in-corona measurements at low latitude.
First mission designed to image the Sun's polar regions in detail; complements Parker Solar Probe's in-corona measurements with high-latitude remote sensing

ESA-led mission with a NASA launch and two instruments (SoloHI and the Heavy Ion Sensor). Where Parker Solar Probe goes closer than anyone has ever been, Solar Orbiter goes higher — using repeated Venus gravity assists over a decade to climb out of the ecliptic toward ~33° heliographic inclination. From that vantage point its instrument suite (PHI, EUI, SPICE, STIX, METIS, SoloHI + four in-situ packages) images the Sun's polar magnetic fields, traces solar-wind acceleration in real time, and links remote and in-situ measurements simultaneously. First perihelion 2020-06-15 at 0.51 AU. Perihelion P5 on 2022-10-12 at 0.29 AU (inside Mercury's perihelion).
